1142.title: Where prayer comes from (CCC 2652–2660)
1142.hook: the word, the liturgy, faith, hope, charity, and today
1142.howItsDone: Catholics draw their prayer from reading scripture, from the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, and from the events of an ordinary day, which some bring to God as they happen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five forms: blessing, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise. Your line was five ways to speak.

Turn on a kitchen tap and water comes out. Simple. Except the water didn't start in the kitchen. Somewhere out of sight there's a reservoir, a main under the street, a pipe in the wall. The tap is only where it shows up. The Catechism asks the same about prayer. If prayer is speaking with God, where does the speaking come from? It names a handful of springs, and the last one on its list is so plain it's easy to miss. Today: where prayer comes from.
screen: `A TAP IN THE KITCHEN.` → `THE WATER STARTS ELSEWHERE.` → `WHERE DOES PRAYER START?`

segments.voice: The Catechism begins back at the well from a few days ago, where Jesus promises water that, in the Douay-Rheims, "shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting." It reads that living water as the Holy Spirit, then asks where we go to draw it. First spring: the word of God. It recalls Saint Ambrose: when we pray, we speak to God; when we read the scriptures, we hear him. Two halves of one conversation. Second: the liturgy. At Mass and in the Church's daily prayer, the Church prays together, and personal prayer takes that liturgy in and makes it its own, during the celebration and after it. Third: three virtues. Faith, which it calls the way in. Hope, in Paul's words: "hope confoundeth not: because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts." And charity, love itself. Then the surprise. The last spring isn't a book or a building. It's today. The Catechism points to a psalm: "To day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts." We learn to pray at certain moments, it says, but the Spirit is offered at all times, in the events of each day. A traffic jam. A waiting room. A child's question over cereal. In this reading, those aren't interruptions of prayer. They're where it can spring up.
screen: `THE WORD OF GOD.` · `THE LITURGY.` · `FAITH, HOPE, CHARITY.` · `TODAY IS A SPRING.`

segments.voice: Don't reach for a holy thought; look at what's actually here: the chair under you, a sound in the next room, something on your mind for later. Pick one. If you pray, bring it to God just as it is, in a sentence of your own; if you don't, simply notice it fully, without fixing it.
Where prayer comes from. In the Catechism, the springs prayer draws on: the word of God, the liturgy, faith, hope and charity, and today itself.
Your line: today is a source. The plainest spring is the one you're standing in. See you tomorrow.

1143.title: The way of prayer (CCC 2663–2672)
1143.hook: to the Father, through Jesus, in the Spirit
1143.howItsDone: Catholic liturgical prayers are usually addressed to the Father and close through Christ in the Holy Spirit; many Catholics also pray directly to Jesus, some with the Jesus Prayer, and call on the Holy Spirit before important work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, where prayer comes from: the word, the liturgy, faith, hope, charity, and today. Your line was today is a source.

An old paper letter needed three things to arrive. A name on the front: who it's for. A stamp and a carrier: how it travels. And something inside worth sending. Get one wrong and it sits in a sorting room forever. Catholic prayer has a shape like that, hiding in plain sight. Listen to how the prayers at Mass end, and the same little pattern keeps turning up: to someone, through someone, in someone. The Catechism lays it out as the way prayer travels. Today: the way of prayer.
screen: `WHO IT'S FOR.` → `HOW IT TRAVELS.` → `TO, THROUGH, IN.`

segments.voice: Start with to. In Catholic teaching, prayer is addressed above all to the Father. Jesus says so at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "if you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you." In my name: that's through. The Catechism says there's no other way of Christian prayer than Christ; alone or together, aloud or silent, it reaches the Father through Jesus. But Jesus isn't only the road. People pray to him directly, by name. Paul writes, "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow." The Catechism describes a prayer from the Christian East, the Jesus Prayer, which you met on day two hundred forty-two: his name joined to a plea for mercy, repeated slowly. It calls calling on his name the simplest way of praying always. Then in. Paul admits, "we know not what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings." When words run out, Catholics say, the Spirit prays inside the one who prays. So the Church invites people to call on the Spirit every day, with the old words "Come, Holy Spirit," especially at the start and the end of something important. To the Father. Through the Son. In the Spirit. Catholics hold this as one God, not three, and the prayer moves the way they believe God does.
screen: `TO THE FATHER.` · `THROUGH JESUS, IN HIS NAME.` · `TO JESUS, BY NAME.` · `IN THE SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: If you pray, turn first to the Father with one short line of your own, then say the name of Jesus slowly, once, then the old words "Come, Holy Spirit," and wait in the quiet after them. If you don't pray, simply notice three directions: what's above you, what's beside you, and what's within.
The way of prayer. In Catholic teaching, prayer goes to the Father, through Jesus and in his name, in the Holy Spirit.
Your line: to, through, in. Three small words, and a whole map of prayer. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1144.title: Guides for prayer (CCC 2685–2690)
1144.hook: families, clergy, religious, prayer groups, spiritual directors
1144.howItsDone: Catholics usually first learn prayer at home, then through parish catechesis, prayer groups and retreats; some meet regularly with a spiritual director to talk about their prayer life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the way of prayer: to the Father, through Jesus, in the Spirit. Your line was to, through, in.

Jesus has just finished praying, off to the side, and his disciples have been watching. They've seen the healings, heard the parables. And when he comes back, what one of them asks for isn't a miracle or an explanation. It's a lesson. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." The ones closest to him, who have seen all of it, still ask to be taught. So who does that teaching now? Today: guides for prayer.
screen: `HE FINISHES PRAYING.` → `LORD, TEACH US TO PRAY.` → `WHO TEACHES NOW?`

segments.voice: The Catechism's answer begins at home. It calls the Christian family the first place prayer is learned, and gives that home a name: the domestic church. A grace before supper, a sign of the cross on a sleeping child's forehead, a parent kneeling by a bed: that's where a child first sees what praying looks like. Paul writes to Timothy of a faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, before it lived in him. Then the Church's ministers. Priests and deacons, the Catechism says, are responsible for forming people in prayer, not only leading it. Next, people in religious life, monks, nuns, sisters and brothers, many of whom have given their lives to prayer; their monasteries and convents keep a rhythm others can join or learn from. Then prayer groups, which the Catechism calls schools of prayer: a few people around a table, a Bible open, a rosary passed around a parish hall. And last, spiritual direction. Some Catholics meet regularly with one wise person, a priest, a sister or a trained lay guide, to talk honestly about their prayer. Drawing on John of the Cross, the Catechism says the choice matters: a guide should be learned, prudent and experienced. Nobody is expected to work prayer out alone in a locked room. Even the disciples, standing next to Jesus, asked.
screen: `THE FAMILY: A DOMESTIC CHURCH.` · `MINISTERS AND RELIGIOUS.` · `PRAYER GROUPS: SCHOOLS OF PRAYER.` · `A SPIRITUAL DIRECTOR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who showed you how to pray, or how to be still, or how to hope: a grandparent, a teacher, a stranger in a pew. Then think of one person who could teach you a little more. If you pray, thank God for the first and ask for courage with the second; if you don't, simply hold them both in mind.

1145.title: Three expressions (CCC 2700–2724)
1145.howItsDone: Catholics pray vocally with the Our Father, the Hail Mary and the prayers of the Mass; meditate through lectio divina and the mysteries of the rosary; and some practice silent contemplation, often in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, guides for prayer: families, ministers, religious, prayer groups, directors. Your line was nobody learns alone.

Noon, in a quiet church, three people in one pew. The first murmurs a prayer under her breath, beads sliding through her fingers. The second has a small Bible open on his knee, reading one line, looking up, reading it again. The third isn't doing anything anyone could see. No book, no words. Just sitting, eyes resting on the tabernacle. From the back of the church they look like three different things. The Catechism says they're three ways of doing one thing. Today: three expressions.
screen: `THREE PEOPLE, ONE PEW.` → `WORDS, A BOOK, NOTHING VISIBLE.` → `ONE THING, THREE WAYS.`

segments.voice: First, vocal prayer: prayer with words, aloud or under the breath. Jesus himself taught one. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thus therefore shall you pray: Our Father who art in heaven." We're bodies as well as spirits, the Catechism says, so prayer naturally comes out through the lips. But the words are meant to carry the heart, not replace it. That's the voice. Second, meditation: the mind at work, a search to understand what God is asking. It usually leans on something: scripture, an icon, a prayer of the liturgy, the writings of the saints. The Catechism names lectio divina, slow holy reading, and the rosary. The model is Mary after the shepherds leave: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Thought, imagination, feeling and desire all get used. That's the mind. Third, contemplation. The Catechism quotes Teresa of Avila: close sharing between friends, taking time to be alone with the one who loves us. And it tells the story you met on day two hundred thirty-two, from the French village of Ars: a peasant who prayed before the tabernacle and said simply, I look at him, and he looks at me. The Catechism calls contemplation a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus. That's the gaze. Three expressions, one prayer; the same person might use all three in a single afternoon.
screen: `VOCAL PRAYER: THE VOICE.` · `MEDITATION: THE MIND.` · `CONTEMPLATION: THE GAZE.` · `THREE EXPRESSIONS, ONE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Voice: say one line of a prayer you know, or of anything that matters to you, slowly, in a whisper. Mind: take one word from that line and turn it over; what does it ask of you today? Gaze: then let the words go and rest your attention, the way the peasant of Ars did, looking and letting yourself be looked at.
Three expressions. In the Catechism: vocal prayer, meditation and contemplation, prayer with the voice, with the mind, and with the gaze.
Your line: voice, mind, gaze. Three ways in, and all of them one prayer. See you tomorrow.

1146.title: The battle of prayer (CCC 2725–2745)
1146.hook: distraction, dryness, lack of faith, and not giving up
1146.howItsDone: Catholics who struggle with distraction or dryness in prayer are usually encouraged by priests and spiritual directors to keep a regular time of prayer anyway, gently returning to it each time the mind wanders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three expressions: vocal prayer, meditation, contemplation. Your line was voice, mind, gaze.

"Pray without ceasing." Three words in Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians. Then the actual attempt. A quiet room, eyes closed, the first line of a prayer. Within a few breaths, a grocery list arrives. Then an email that needs answering. Then an old argument, replayed with a better comeback. Minutes later, the prayer is still on its first line. It would be easy to decide you're bad at praying, and stop. Back on day twenty, Teresa of Avila admitted prayer went that way for her for years. The Catechism has a word for it, and it isn't failure. Today: the battle of prayer.
screen: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.` → `A GROCERY LIST ARRIVES.` → `NOT FAILURE. A BATTLE.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says it plainly: prayer is a battle. Not against God, but against ourselves, our surroundings, and, in its words, the wiles of the tempter. It isn't a sign something's broken; it's what praying is like. Then it names the troubles. Distraction first, and the advice is surprising: don't hunt distractions down. Chasing them is falling into their trap. Just turn back to the heart, and notice what the distraction shows you, because it shows what you're attached to. The grocery list isn't the enemy. It's information. Next, dryness: prayer with no taste at all, no feeling, no words. The Catechism calls this a moment of sheer faith, staying with Jesus in his agony and in the tomb, and reaches for his own image: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die," it remains alone. Something is happening under the soil. Then lack of faith, which shows up less as open doubt than in what we put first, when other cares that seem urgent crowd ahead of prayer. And acedia, a listless weariness about spiritual things. The answer to all of it is the same: persevere. Luke introduces one of Jesus's stories this way: "that we ought always to pray, and not to faint." A widow keeps coming back to an unjust judge until he finally gives her justice. The point isn't that God is like that judge. The point is the widow. She keeps coming back.
screen: `PRAYER IS A BATTLE.` · `DISTRACTION: TURN BACK.` · `DRYNESS: SHEER FAITH.` · `THE WIDOW KEEPS COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose one short line, the first words of the Our Father or just the name of Jesus; if you don't, choose your breath, and rest on it. When your mind wanders, don't scold it: name where it went in one word, list, worry, plan, and come back. Each return is the practice, not a failure of it.
The battle of prayer. In the Catechism, the struggle with distraction, dryness, lack of faith and weariness, met by humble watchfulness and perseverance.
Your line: keep coming back. Every single return counts, even the hundredth. Same time tomorrow.

1147.title: Jesus's prayer at the supper (CCC 2746–2751)
1147.hook: John 17, the prayer of the hour
1147.tomorrow: The whole gospel in a prayer
1147.howItsDone: Catholics hear John 17 read at Mass in the weeks of Easter, and its words "that they all may be one" are sometimes used at gatherings for Christian unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the battle of prayer: distraction, dryness, weariness, and the widow who wouldn't quit. Your line was keep coming back.

The supper is over. The feet have been washed. Judas has gone out into the night. For chapters, John's Gospel has let Jesus talk to his friends at the table: about a vine and its branches, a helper who will come, a sorrow that will turn to joy. Then, with the garden and the arrest a short walk away, he stops talking to them. He lifts his eyes and talks to his Father, out loud, with them still in the room. They get to overhear it. So do we. Today: Jesus's prayer at the supper.
screen: `THE SUPPER IS OVER.` → `HE STOPS TALKING TO THEM.` → `THEY OVERHEAR HIM PRAY.`

segments.voice: John 17 opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "Father, the hour is come, glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee." Earlier in John, his hour had not yet come. Now it has. The Catechism calls this the prayer of the hour of Jesus, and says Christian tradition rightly names it his priestly prayer: a high priest praying on the edge of offering himself. It moves outward in rings. First he prays for himself, to finish the work he was given. Then for the friends in the room, and here's the line that surprises: "I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from evil." Not their escape. Kept, right where they are. Then the ring widens past the room and past that night: "And not for them only do I pray, but for them also who through their word shall believe in me." Catholics hear every later believer in that line, down to today. And what he asks for them is "That they all may be one." The Catechism adds that this prayer, like his sacrifice, reaches to the end of time. And the Our Father's requests are already folded in: the Father's name, his work finished, his people kept from evil. In the Catholic reading, the prayer he taught and the prayer he prayed are one.
screen: `FATHER, THE HOUR IS COME.` · `KEEP THEM FROM EVIL.` · `FOR THOSE WHO WILL BELIEVE.` · `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, read John chapter seventeen slowly, as far as you get; if not, hold one line: "That they all may be one." Notice who's in each ring: himself, his friends, people not yet born. If you pray, let yourself be one of the ones he prays for; if you don't, just stay with what he asks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus's prayer at the supper: John 17, the prayer of the hour. Your line was his prayer for us.

Could a whole faith fit on an index card? An early Christian writer named Tertullian thought one already did. In a work on prayer, he made a bold claim about the prayer Jesus taught, the Our Father, which you first met on day eleven: in it is a summary of the whole gospel. Not a piece of it. The whole. The Catechism opens one of its articles on the Lord's Prayer with his words. All week it has walked around prayer: its springs, its way, its guides, its expressions, its battles, and Jesus's own prayer. Now it opens the prayer itself. Today: the whole gospel in a prayer.
screen: `A FAITH ON AN INDEX CARD?` → `TERTULLIAN'S BOLD CLAIM.` → `THE WEEK ARRIVES AT ONE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Tertullian's Latin is breviarium totius evangelii: a short summary of the whole gospel. Test the claim against the prayer, in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven." Then bread, forgiveness, temptation, and deliverance from evil. Now hold the Gospels next to it. Jesus begins preaching, in Matthew, with "the kingdom of heaven is at hand." There's the second line. He feeds crowds with a few loaves: the bread. He forgives sinners and tells of a father running to meet a lost son: the forgiveness. He's tempted in the desert, and frees people from evil spirits: the last lines. The prayer runs through the Gospel like a spine. The Catechism adds a practical thought from Tertullian. Jesus also said ask and you shall receive, and everyone has needs of their own. So this prayer comes first, as the foundation, and the rest of our asking is built on it. A Catholic praying for a sick friend isn't setting the Our Father aside; it goes underneath. And it's short enough for a child to learn by heart, said at Mass, at a bedside, in a rosary, under the breath at a red light. Small enough to carry anywhere. Big enough, Tertullian said, to hold everything.
